Why alert volume is an engineering problem

RELIABILITY · 6 MIN READ · SEPTEMBER 2026

An alert is supposed to change what an engineer does.

If an alert fires often enough that people learn to ignore it, the system has stopped communicating. The problem is no longer just noisy monitoring; it is a reliability problem.

The useful question is not “How do we make fewer alerts?” It is “Which failures actually require a human response, and how do we make those signals trustworthy?”

In production, reducing alert noise starts with looking at the incidents behind the alerts. Some signals are low-value. Some are false errors. Some represent real failures but are better handled automatically. And some important failure modes are not being monitored well enough.

The work is a loop: understand the failure, decide who or what should respond, improve the signal, and document the operational path.

The result is not simply a quieter PagerDuty queue. It is a system where an engineer can trust that an alert deserves attention.
